paper.title: A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions
paper.research_summary: We present Matbench Discovery as an example evaluation framework for machine learning energy models, here applied as pre-filters to first-principles computed data in a high-throughput search for stable inorganic crystals.

task.objective: To accelerate high-throughput computational materials discovery by using machine learning models as efficient pre-filters for DFT calculations, specifically to identify thermodynamically stable inorganic crystals.
target_properties: distance to convex hull phase diagram
constraints: models must predict relaxed energy from unrelaxed structures
test input is unrelaxed structure only
avoid circular dependency with DFT relaxation
output_goal: classification of thermodynamic stability (on or below convex hull)

evidence.text: We present Matbench Discovery as an example evaluation framework for machine learning energy models, here applied as pre-filters to first-principles computed data in a high-throughput search for stable inorganic crystals.
Our work aims to identify the state-of-the-art model by proposing an evaluation framework that closely simulates a real-world discovery campaign guided by ML models.
This work proposes a benchmark task designed to address four fundamental challenges that we believe are essential to justify the effort of experimentally validating ML predictions:

stages.stage_goal: Collect large-scale, diverse DFT-computed data on inorganic crystals for model training.

evidence.text: We define the MP3 v.2022.10.28 database release as the maximum allowed training set for any compliant model submission.

The MP is a widely used database of inorganic materials properties that have been calculated using high-throughput ab initio methods. At the time of writing, the MP database3 has grown to ~154,000 crystals, covering diverse chemistries and providing relaxed and initial structures as well as the relaxation trajectory for every entry.

stages.stage_goal: Obtain prospectively generated, out-of-distribution test data simulating real discovery workflow.

evidence.text: Our test set consists of the unrelaxed structures in the WBM dataset50.

The WBM dataset50 consists of 257,487 structures generated via chemical similarity-based elemental substitution of MP source structures followed by DFT relaxation and calculating each crystal’s convex hull distance.

stages.stage_name_raw: Cleaning and protostructure filtering of WBM test set
stages.stage_goal: Remove data leakage between training and test sets by eliminating protostructure matches and pathological outliers.

evidence.text: To control for the potential adverse effects of leakage between the MP training set and the WBM test set, we cleaned the WBM test set based on protostructure matching.

First we removed 524 pathological structures in WBM based on formation energies being larger than 5 eV per atom or smaller than −5 eV per atom. We then removed from the WBM test set all examples where the final protostructure of a WBM material matched the final protostructure of an MP material. In total, 11,175 materials were cleaned using this filter.

stages.stage_goal: Generate stability labels by computing each material's distance to the convex hull of the MP training set.

evidence.text: Their target values are the PBE formation energies of the corresponding DFT-relaxed structures.
Throughout this work, we define stability as being on or below the convex hull of the MP training set (EMP hull dist ≤ 0).

The convex hull distance of a relaxed structure is chosen as the measure of its thermodynamic stability, rather than the formation energy, as it informs the decision on whether to pursue a potential candidate crystal.

stages.stage_name_raw: Training ML models on MP data
stages.stage_goal: Train diverse ML models—including universal interatomic potentials and energy-only predictors—on MP training data to predict relaxed energy from unrelaxed inputs.
stage_output: 13 trained ML models (e.g., EquiformerV2+DeNS, ORB, SevenNet, MACE, CHGNet, etc.)

evidence.text: To test a wide variety of methodologies proposed for learning the potential energy landscape, our initial benchmark release includes 13 models.
We enforce only that at test time, all models must make predictions on the convex hull distance of the relaxed structure with only the unrelaxed structure as input.

stages.stage_name_raw: Ranking hypothetical materials by predicted stability
stages.stage_goal: Use trained models to rank WBM test structures by predicted hull distance to simulate prospective discovery campaign ordering.
stage_output: ranked list of materials ordered by predicted hull distance (most to least stable)

evidence.text: For each model, we iterate through that list and calculate at each step the precision and recall of correctly identified stable materials. This simulates exactly how these models would be used in a prospective materials discovery campaign...
A typical discovery campaign will rank hypothetical materials by model-predicted hull distance from most to least stable and validate the most stable predictions first.

stages.stage_name_raw: Screening top-ranked candidates for stability classification
stages.stage_goal: Evaluate model performance by assessing classification accuracy (stable/unstable) on progressively larger subsets of top-ranked candidates.

evidence.text: This simulates exactly how these models would be used in a prospective materials discovery campaign and reveals how a model’s performance changes as a function of the discovery campaign length.
The discovery acceleration factor (DAF) quantifies how many times more effective a model is at finding stable structures compared with random selection from the test set.

stages.stage_name_raw: Benchmarking model performance on classification metrics
stages.stage_goal: Compare models using task-relevant classification metrics (F1, DAF, precision, recall) rather than regression metrics alone.
stage_output: comparative analysis of UIP vs. energy-only models

evidence.text: Table 1 shows performance metrics for all models included in the initial release of Matbench Discovery reported on the unique protostructure subset.
We highlight a misalignment between commonly used regression metrics and more task-relevant classification metrics for materials discovery.

Our results demonstrate that accurate regressors are susceptible to unexpectedly high false-positive rates if those accurate predictions lie close to the decision boundary at 0 eV per atom above the convex hull.
